Taxation
taks-AY-shun
n. (an assessment laid on persons or property)
Hebrew erek, an estimate or valuation, from arak, to set in order or appraise — the assessed rating of a man's worth for the levy. Latin taxatio, a valuing, from taxare, to appraise.

Biblical Definition

And Jehoiakim gave the silver and the gold to Pharaoh; but he taxed the land to give the money according to the commandment of Pharaoh: he exacted the silver and the gold of the people of the land, of every one according to his taxation, to give it unto Pharaohnechoh. The verse sits immediately after the death of Josiah and the end of his reformation, and the contrast is deliberate. Josiah had torn out the idols and kept the law; his son pays tribute to Egypt and raises it from his own people. The mechanism is described exactly: an assessment was set on every man, and the money was exacted. Scripture does not condemn taxation as such — the Lord told his hearers to render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and Paul commands Christians to pay tribute to whom tribute is due. What this passage exposes is a particular arrangement: a king raising money from his own people to purchase the favour of a foreign power that had conquered them. Jehoiakim had no independence to protect and no reform to fund. The judgment on him is given in the chapter's framing, since the writer of Kings keeps his own accounts and records that Jehoiakim did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD. The verse is a small, precise portrait of what follows a reformation when the next generation does not hold it: the outward machinery of the state continues, and its burden falls where it always falls.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): the act of laying a tax, or of imposing taxes on the subjects of a state; the sum imposed; a rate or assessment.

expand to see more

TAXATION, n. The act of laying a tax, or of imposing taxes on the subjects of a state by government.

TAXATION, n. Tax; sum imposed; the rate or assessment laid on a person or estate.

TAX, n. A rate or sum of money assessed on the person or property of a citizen by government, for the use of the nation or state.

EXACT, v.t. To force or compel to pay or yield; to demand or require authoritatively.

TRIBUTE, n. An annual or stated sum of money or other valuable thing, paid by one prince or nation to another, either for peace or protection.

Key Scripture

2 Kings 23:35 — "And Jehoiakim gave the silver and the gold to Pharaoh; but he taxed the land to give the money according to the commandment of Pharaoh: he exacted the silver and the gold of the people of the land, of every one according to his taxation, to give it unto Pharaohnechoh."

2 Kings 23:25 — "And like unto him was there no king before him, that turned to the LORD with all his heart, and with all his soul, and with all his might, according to all the law of Moses; neither after him arose there any like him."

2 Kings 23:24 — "Moreover the workers with familiar spirits, and the wizards, and the images, and the idols, and all the abominations that were spied in the land of Judah and in Jerusalem, did Josiah put away, that he might perform the words of the law which were written in the book that Hilkiah the priest found in the house of the LORD."

Luke 2:1 — "And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed."

Modern Corruption

Scripture is recruited for whichever fiscal politics a reader already holds; what the Bible actually supplies is a doctrine of spheres, a command to pay what is owed, and a standing warning about rulers who exact from their own.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live temptation is to make the Bible a partisan document on tax policy in either direction. It will not serve. The Lord commanded the rendering of Caesar's coin to Caesar, and Paul commands tribute, custom, fear, and honour to whom they are due — under a pagan empire, with no suggestion that its rates required Christian approval first. Scripture equally records prophets denouncing rulers who devour their people and a king whose exactions are set down as part of his indictment. The principle to recover is the doctrine of spheres: family, church, and state each have authority God has given and limits God has set, and a state that swells past its sphere is a biblical concern whatever the rate.

The second thing this verse teaches is about generations. Josiah's reformation was thorough — the writer says there was no king like him before or after — and it did not survive his son. The idols came back, the tribute was paid, and the people bore it. Reformation is never inherited. Every generation receives the outward forms and must be brought to the thing itself, which is why Scripture places such weight on households teaching children and why the found book in the house of the LORD is the hinge of Josiah's whole reign. What is not taught afresh is lost, and what follows the loss is usually described in the flat administrative language of this verse.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew erek (H6187), a valuation or assessment; arak (H6186), to appraise; nagas (H5065), to exact or drive; keceph (H3701), silver or money.

expand to see more

Hebrew erek (H6187) — an estimate, an assessed rating; rendered taxation.

Hebrew arak (H6186) — to set in order, to value; the root of the assessment.

Hebrew nagas (H5065) — to press, to drive, to exact; rendered exacted.

Hebrew keceph (H3701) — silver, money; what was taken of the people of the land.

Greek apographo (G583) — to enrol, to register; behind all the world should be taxed.

Usage

"“of every one according to his taxation” — an assessment set on each man."

"“he exacted the silver and the gold of the people” — raised to pay a foreign king."

"“neither after him arose there any like him” — what the next reign lost."
